props.title: Small Change
props.initialSlug: Charming slice of life through children's eyes in France

sections.content: François Truffaut's Small Change (1976) masterfully captures childhood with documentary-like authenticity. Like his landmark The 400 Blows (1959), it observes kids being kids - playing, learning, testing boundaries - but trades Antoine Doinel's singular story for an expansive mosaic of interconnected youth experiences in Thiers, France. The film's genius lies in Truffaut's refusal to sentimentalize or condescend. He shows children as complex, resilient beings navigating their world with humor and ingenuity, even amid hardship.

sections.content: Truffaut's approach to directing children set new standards. Unlike The Little Rascals (1922-1944) or overly precious Hollywood productions, he let kids be naturally mischievous and unpredictable. This influenced later classics like Ponette (1996) and The Florida Project (2017), which similarly capture authentic childhood experiences. His documentary-style technique, mixing professional and non-professional child actors, creates an almost ethnographic study of youth culture.

The film's episodic structure revolutionized how childhood could be portrayed on screen. Rather than following conventional plot arcs, Small Change weaves together seemingly random moments that build into a profound tapestry of growing up. This technique later influenced works like Boyhood (2014) and The Kid with a Bike (2011), which similarly resist traditional narrative in favor of authentic childhood experiences. sections.content: The DNA of Small Change runs through many modern films about childhood. Sean Baker's The Florida Project (2017) shares its keen eye for how children create adventure in any environment. Céline Sciamma's Tomboy (2011) echoes Truffaut's sensitive handling of complex childhood identity. These films continue the tradition of treating young protagonists with serious artistic consideration rather than mere cuteness.
